input.subject: POC: Carefully exposing information without authentication

verdict_reasoning: The proposal fails at level 1b on already-exists-1. Message #13 itself describes a working script on a separate port, and message #18 recommends that route, so the thread shows the external approach takes setup but does the job. Demand for core placement rests on one F5 site (demand-1), and no operator asks for the version or sysid endpoints (demand-2). Meeting the objection means a separate listener or service, which is a different proposal.

brief.title: Answer unauthenticated HTTP requests for role, version and system identifier
brief.problem: HA systems, load balancers and security scanners need to know whether a server is primary or replica, or which version it runs. Today they must log in and run pg_is_in_recovery(), or guess the version from error output after a bad login. Without Patroni, users write wrapper scripts and create a database user just to answer "is this the primary?".
brief.proposed_design: A new GUC expose_information lists which facts the server may reveal. Right after fork, before the startup packet, the backend peeks at the first bytes in non-blocking mode; on an exact match of a known HTTP request it sends a minimal HTTP/1.1 response and exits. Bytes that do not match stay in the socket buffer and normal startup and authentication continue.
user_visible_surface: GUC expose_information (string, comma-separated: role, version, sysid; default empty; changes with a reload).
HTTP endpoints on the Postgres port: HEAD /replica and HEAD /primary return status 200 or 503 with no body.
GET /replica and GET /primary return 1 or 0; GET /version returns server_version_num; GET /sysid returns the system identifier.
New log message "failed to send information to client" when send() fails.
author_claims: The facts exposed are low-impact and not a security leak.
HEAD /replica and HEAD /primary are drop-in replacements for the same Patroni REST API calls.
GET /version gives scanners an exact answer instead of a guess from source line numbers in error messages.
Skipping authentication and backend setup makes the check lightweight; early tests showed barely measurable postmaster impact.
Normal connections are unaffected even when expose_information is set.
brief.thread_state: Tom Lane, Daniel Gustafsson and Jacob Champion object to any work on client input before authentication; Tom doubts it will ever be committed, and Jacob calls mixing HTTP and the Postgres protocol on one port a nonstarter. Andres Freund's points on direct TLS, man-in-the-middle trust and a separate interface are answered only partly.
unclear: The proposal does not say how it prevents cross-protocol attacks between HTTP and the Postgres protocol on one port.
Direct TLS connections are not handled, and the proposal does not say what happens to them.
The proposal does not say whether the endpoints can be limited to some addresses or interfaces, or controlled by pg_hba.conf.
No numbers show the cost of fork and exit per request, or the effect of a flood of such requests on connection slots.
The cause of the Windows CI failure after reload is unknown; the test uses a sleep.

objections.title: A small separate service already answers this without core changes
objections.failure_scenario: A site with a load balancer and no Patroni enables expose_information to avoid writing a health-check script. Core now carries an unauthenticated HTTP responder on the Postgres port permanently. A side-by-side service would have given the same 200/503 answer and could be bound to a management interface.
objections.argument: The need is met today by the Patroni REST API, or by a short script that runs pg_is_in_recovery() and serves the result on another port, as message #13 describes and message #18 recommends. Libpq clients can already choose the primary with target_session_attrs. Message #13 calls the script approach "a whole lot of trouble", which is a convenience argument. The proposal does not show that the external approach is impossible, only that it takes setup.
objections.author_must_show: What does a load balancer gain from core placement that a separate health-check service on its own port and interface cannot give?

critic.reasoning: Message #13 itself describes a working script on a separate port, and message #18 recommends that route. The thread shows that this takes setup, but not that it cannot do the job.

objections.title: Demand rests on one consulting client's load balancer
objections.failure_scenario: The project ships unauthenticated pre-startup handling of client bytes for a small group of sites that run no Patroni and use a load balancer that cannot speak the Postgres protocol. Every later change to backend startup, direct TLS or the protocol must keep this path safe, even though few installations turn it on.
objections.argument: The only concrete field report is one F5 BIG-IP client in message #13. No other user in the 18 messages asks for the feature, and the thread cites no -general or -bugs reports. The workaround already works, as message #13 itself describes: a small script on a separate port that runs pg_is_in_recovery(). Message #18 suggests the same separate service. The author finds that workaround inconvenient, but that alone does not show the group is large.
objections.author_must_show: Which independent users or HA and load balancer vendors need an unauthenticated role check on the Postgres port, and why can a separate small service not serve them?

critic.reasoning: The only field report is the one F5 client in message #13, and no other user in the thread asks for the feature. Patroni's REST API shows the need for HTTP role checks, but not for one on the Postgres port.

objections.title: Version and sysid endpoints have no stated user who needs them
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA enables role for a load balancer and adds version as well, because the documentation presents it as harmless. Anyone who can reach the port can then read the exact minor version without logging in, and match it against known CVEs.
objections.argument: The reason given for GET /version is that scanners guess the version from error output today (messages #1 and #14), so the people who gain are the scanners, not the operators of the database. No operator in the thread asks for the exact version to be readable without a login. GET /sysid is described as useful for checking that a cluster is the same one (message #1), but no tool or user is named who needs this without authentication. Message #13 says people want the version or the role, but the only workflow shown uses the role.
objections.author_must_show: Which operators, not scanners, need the exact version or the system identifier without authentication, and what do they use today?

critic.reasoning: The thread names scanners as the users of GET /version and no tool that needs GET /sysid without a login. Message #13 shows a workflow only for role.

other_surviving.title: HTTP on the Postgres port adds a permanent second wire contract
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A later release adds a new pre-startup request or changes direct TLS negotiation. Its first bytes have to be checked against the fixed list of HTTP request lines, and tools that probe the port with HTTP depend on those request lines staying stable. Any mismatch shows up as a client that gets the wrong protocol's reply.
other_surviving.argument: Today the first bytes a client sends can only be a startup packet, SSLRequest, GSSENCRequest, cancel request or a TLS ClientHello, all defined by the Postgres protocol. The patch adds HTTP request lines to that set and documents them as a drop-in interface, so the project would have to keep them indefinitely. Jacob Champion calls mixing the two protocols on one port a nonstarter in message #18, and the proposal does not say why a separate listener or service cannot meet the same need.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why can a separate port or external service, which keeps the Postgres wire protocol unchanged, not serve the F5 and scanner cases?

critic.reasoning: The commit message documents the HTTP request lines as a drop-in interface on the Postgres port, and message #18 names this as the core problem. Message #12 does not say why a separate listener cannot serve the same need.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Local recovery state is not the leader answer Patroni gives
other_surviving.failure_scenario: After a failover, the old primary is partitioned from the HA system but still reachable by the load balancer. It is not in recovery, so HEAD /primary returns 200 on both nodes. The F5 then sends writes to two primaries, and the operator finds out when timelines diverge and the old node needs pg_rewind or a rebuild.
other_surviving.argument: The patch answers /primary and /replica from RecoveryInProgress() alone (messages #1 and #14), which is a fact about one node. A cluster manager's endpoint also reflects who holds leadership, so the claim that these are drop-in replacements for the Patroni calls (message #14, the docs hunk) does not hold. Message #13 aims at exactly the setup without a cluster manager, where nothing else fences the old primary. Message #12 accepts that the answer cannot be trusted against tampering, but this failure needs no attacker.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How does a load balancer that uses HEAD /primary avoid routing writes to a demoted or partitioned old primary that still reports it is not in recovery?

critic.reasoning: The docs call HEAD /primary a drop-in replacement, but RecoveryInProgress() is a local fact and Patroni's answer depends on the leader lock. A script that runs pg_is_in_recovery() has the same limit, so the fix is in the documented claim.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Unauthenticated role answer can be spoofed to misroute writes
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An F5 polls HEAD /primary in plain text. An attacker on the path answers 200 for a replica, or 503 for the real primary. The load balancer then sends writes to the wrong server or takes the primary out of service, and the DBA finds out from application errors.
other_surviving.argument: The author calls the data "non-critical" (message #12), but message #13 presents role as the input for routing decisions in a load balancer. That makes the integrity of the answer critical, whatever its secrecy. Andres asked how a coordinator can trust plain text that can be intercepted (message #11). The answer was "They cannot", and direct TLS is "Not handled" (message #12).
other_surviving.author_must_show: How can a load balancer that routes on HEAD /primary verify that the answer came from the server, given that the requests use no TLS and no authentication?

critic.reasoning: Message #13 presents the role answer as input for load balancer routing, and message #12 confirms the answer cannot be trusted and that direct TLS is not handled. Telling such sites not to use the feature leaves out the main use case.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: No address or pg_hba control over who receives version and sysid
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A DBA enables expose_information = 'role,version' for one internal load balancer. Every host that can reach 5432, including internet scanners, now gets the exact server_version_num. That tells them which minor releases are missing and which known vulnerabilities to try first.
other_surviving.argument: The GUC switches each fact on or off for every client. pg_hba.conf is never consulted, and the proposal gives no way to limit by address or interface. Andres suggested a smaller set of interfaces (message #11), and the author did not take this up (message #12). The argument that scanners already guess the version (message #1) does not justify giving an exact answer to every host that can reach the port.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How can a DBA expose role to one load balancer address without also exposing version and sysid to every client that can reach the port?

critic.reasoning: The GUC is global and the check runs before pg_hba.conf is consulted. Message #12 did not take up the request in message #11 for a smaller set of interfaces.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Core would follow Patroni's REST API semantics indefinitely
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An operator moves a load balancer from Patroni's /replica to Postgres's /replica because the docs call it a drop-in replacement. Patroni's endpoint also considers lag or tags, but the core endpoint reports only RecoveryInProgress(). The balancer then sends reads to a replica that Patroni would have excluded, and the operator finds out from stale results.
other_surviving.argument: The docs and commit message call HEAD /replica and HEAD /primary drop-in replacements for Patroni, which is an interface the project does not control (message #14). Message #13 already admits it will never fully match Patroni, so users will ask for more endpoints and parameters. Each one adds to an unauthenticated surface that has no pg_hba.conf or interface control (message #11). Endpoint names shipped in a release cannot be withdrawn without breaking monitoring setups.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which rule limits the endpoint set, and how does the proposal avoid becoming bound to Patroni's API as it changes?

critic.reasoning: The docs name Patroni compatibility as a property of the endpoints, and message #13 says they will never match the full API. The proposal gives no rule that limits the endpoint set.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: No committer in the thread is willing to own pre-authentication code
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A security report arrives about cross-protocol confusion or about exhausting connection slots with HTTP requests. A committer then has to fix pre-authentication code that the thread's security-aware reviewers declined to review in detail (message #18). Direct TLS is still unhandled (message #12), and the cause of the Windows test failure is unknown (message #17).
other_surviving.argument: The entry has gone through six CommitFests, and no committer has endorsed the design. Message #4 and message #11 raise concerns about blocking and spurious failures. Message #12 answers those with "good enough" and an instruction to retry, which is a weak base for code that runs before authentication. No measurements show the cost of one fork per health check, or the effect on postmaster children when many load balancers poll every second.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which committer familiar with backend startup and protocol security will review and maintain this, and what numbers show the cost of one fork per health check?

critic.reasoning: No committer in the thread supports the design, and three reviewers object to it. Two details do not hold: message #13 added non-blocking reads and a send timeout, and unauthenticated clients can already hold a backend until authentication_timeout.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Pre-auth endpoints bypass pg_hba.conf and per-address limits
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA's pg_hba.conf rejects every host outside the application subnet. The DBA then sets expose_information = 'role,version,sysid' for a load balancer. Every host that can reach the port, including internet scanners, now gets the version and system identifier, and pg_hba.conf has no rule that can stop it.
refuted.argument: Postgres controls who may reach a server before login through listen_addresses and pg_hba.conf. The single expose_information setting works outside both. Andres Freund asked in message #11 for the endpoints to be limited to a smaller set of interfaces, and message #12 replied that it was not clear what that would mean in practice.
refuted.author_must_show: How does an administrator allow the load balancer's address to use these endpoints while denying all other hosts, using existing Postgres access controls?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of security-3. This version also says the setting works outside listen_addresses, but the endpoints answer only on addresses the server listens on.

refuted.title: No TLS path, so the check works only as plaintext HTTP
refuted.failure_scenario: A site that requires TLS sets up an HTTPS health monitor against port 5432. The TLS ClientHello does not match any endpoint and goes into normal startup, so the monitor always reports failure. The only working option is plaintext, where a man-in-the-middle can flip the primary or replica answer and the load balancer then routes writes to a standby.
refuted.argument: Message #12 says direct TLS is not handled and that sites worried about interception should not use the feature. Postgres now supports direct TLS for normal connections, so a new pre-auth interface that has no TLS form is a departure from that direction. The answer is also used for routing decisions, so a tampered reply has a cost beyond leaking information.
refuted.author_must_show: How do sites that require TLS on every connection use these endpoints, and what stops a tampered role answer from misrouting traffic?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of security-2, which states the integrity problem of a plaintext role answer more directly. The missing TLS form is the same gap seen from the monitor's side.

refuted.title: Claimed Patroni drop-in compatibility does not match the check performed
refuted.failure_scenario: A user points a load balancer's existing Patroni HEAD /replica check at Postgres. The patch answers 200 for any server in recovery, including a standby that has lost its upstream. The load balancer keeps sending reads to a standby that has stopped replaying WAL, and the user notices only when stale data is reported.
refuted.argument: The documentation calls HEAD /replica and HEAD /primary a drop-in replacement for Patroni, but the endpoints only test RecoveryInProgress(). Patroni's endpoints reflect its own view of cluster state. Message #13 already says the endpoints will never be a full replacement for Patroni, so the docs promise compatibility with an external API that the project does not control.
refuted.author_must_show: Which Patroni endpoint semantics are kept exactly, and who updates the Postgres side when Patroni changes them?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1. Its scenario is also weaker, because Patroni's plain /replica check does not test replication lag unless the caller asks for it.

refuted.title: Second protocol on the Postgres port constrains future wire changes
refuted.failure_scenario: A later release adds a new pre-startup negotiation, as direct TLS did. Its authors must check that no client byte prefix can match the HTTP strings and that no HTTP reply can be read as a Postgres message. HTTPS health checks that send a TLS ClientHello get a failed handshake, and the operator sees this only when the check fails.
refuted.argument: The design gives the first bytes on the Postgres port two meanings, and every future change to connection startup must take that into account. Message #18 calls this a nonstarter because of cross-protocol attacks. Message #11 asks about direct TLS and a separate interface, and message #12 answers "Not handled" and does not say what a smaller set would be. Connection poolers and TLS-terminating proxies placed in front of the server also do not pass these requests through, so the endpoint is not reachable in those setups.
refuted.author_must_show: Why must this run on the same port and in the same startup path as the Postgres protocol, and not as a separate listener or service as message #18 suggests?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1 for the wire contract and of security-2 for the missing TLS path. Poolers that do not pass the request through are a limit of the feature and break nothing.

refuted.title: HTTP and the Postgres protocol share one port before authentication
refuted.failure_scenario: An attacker who can reach port 5432 sends crafted bytes that one parser reads as HTTP and the other as a startup packet. Any later change to either path can open a cross-protocol hole. Nobody notices until a security report arrives, and by then every release with the feature is affected.
refuted.argument: The patch reads and acts on client bytes before the startup packet is processed, which is the first pre-authentication input handling outside the protocol. Daniel (message #15), Tom (message #16) and Jacob (message #18) object to the idea itself, and Jacob calls cross-protocol attacks the reason. The author's answer in message #17 is bounded strncmp and fixed outputs. That covers this version of the code, not the lasting duty to check every future change to backend startup against HTTP.
refuted.author_must_show: What design keeps HTTP handling off the Postgres listening socket, or what argument shows that no future change to startup can create a cross-protocol hole?

critic.reasoning: The patch matches exact strings and exits, so the same bytes never reach both parsers; "GET " read as a startup packet length is rejected as too large. The duty to check future startup changes is covered by standards-compat-1.

refuted.title: Health-check service belongs outside the backend startup path
refuted.failure_scenario: A site enables expose_information so its load balancer can find the primary. A later release changes connection startup, for example a new negotiation step. That change must also keep the HTTP peek path working on the same socket, and nobody outside the original author knows to check it.
refuted.argument: The need in message #13 is real, but a small local service can answer it today with its own address, TLS and access rules, as message #18 suggests. The patch puts HTTP matching ahead of the startup packet in backend_startup.c, and three committers object to any pre-authentication input handling (messages #15, #16, #18). Core gains a second wire protocol on the client port without a general mechanism others can reuse. The author's reply in message #9 explains why a libpq option is not enough, but not why an external service fails.
refuted.author_must_show: What does an in-core endpoint on the client port provide that a small separate service or extension with its own listener cannot?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1 for the external service argument and of standards-compat-1 for the burden on future startup changes.

refuted.title: A second protocol on the port instead of extending the startup packet
refuted.failure_scenario: Future work on the startup path, such as direct TLS, protocol negotiation or new startup messages, must also keep HTTP prefix matching correct on the same socket. A reviewer of a later startup change can miss the HTTP branch, and nothing fails loudly when that happens.
refuted.argument: Message #8 proposes the existing mechanism: a startup-packet option, read in ProcessStartupPacket() and answered through pg_isready. Message #9 rejects it because systems that do not speak the protocol could not use it. That answer only covers tools that cannot run pg_isready or a sidecar, and message #12 says direct TLS connections are not handled. A committer would likely prefer extending pg_isready over a parallel HTTP path.
refuted.author_must_show: Which deployed tools can neither run pg_isready nor reach a sidecar service, and why can a startup-packet option not serve them?

critic.reasoning: Message #9 answers this: a startup-packet option cannot serve an HTTP-only monitor without a libpq client or a sidecar. The sidecar alternative is already-exists-1, and the burden on later startup changes is standards-compat-1.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The role endpoints report RecoveryInProgress() on primaries and standbys, and load balancers would route on that answer.

touch_points.label: wire protocol
touch_points.reason: The backend accepts HTTP request lines as first bytes on the Postgres port, next to the startup packet.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The patch adds the string GUC expose_information with the options role, version and sysid.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The server answers before authentication and before pg_hba.conf is consulted, in plain text.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Documented HTTP endpoints, described as Patroni drop-in replacements, must stay stable and be checked against every later startup change.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: When the GUC is set, every new connection gets a non-blocking peek in backend_startup.c, and each probe costs a fork.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: A separate health-check service or the Patroni REST API gives the same answer outside core.

questions: What does a load balancer gain from an endpoint on the Postgres port that a separate health-check service on its own port and interface cannot give?
Which independent users or load balancer vendors, beyond the one F5 site in message #13, ask for an unauthenticated role check on the Postgres port?
Which operators, as opposed to scanners, need the exact version or the system identifier without a login, and what do they use today?
What happens to a direct TLS connection when expose_information is set, and how does the design prevent cross-protocol attacks between HTTP and the Postgres protocol?
What does one fork and exit per probe cost, and how does a flood of such probes affect connection slots?

committability.owner_note: Tom Lane, Daniel Gustafsson and Jacob Champion take part, but all three object to input handling before authentication. The owner would need to know backend startup and protocol security, and nobody has offered.
committability.liability: The owner signs for unauthenticated input handling in backend startup and for HTTP endpoint names that monitoring setups depend on, in every release that ships them. Each later change to connection startup or direct TLS must be checked against the HTTP path.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted revised patches through at least message #14, answered reviews, and moved the entry through six CommitFests.

priority.reason: The shown demand is one site that has a load balancer and no cluster manager, while the cost is a permanent HTTP interface before authentication on the Postgres port. The 25 KiB patch is small, but it changes backend_startup.c, and the thread points to a separate listener or service.

provisional_note: Only 3 of 18 messages and no code were read. The exact-match claim, the socket state restore, the send timeout and the Windows failure after reload could not be checked.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Implementing OCSP Stapling for Server certificate status verification
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds OCSP stapling for the server certificate: a new server setting `ssl_ocsp_file` points to an OCSP response that the DBA fetches in advance, and the server staples it during the TLS handshake. A new libpq connection parameter (`sslocspstapling`) makes the client request the stapled response, check it, and reject the connection when the certificate is not good.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No closing message is shown, so the visible messages do not state the final reason. The last messages question whether the feature is still useful, because OCSP is becoming optional and Let's Encrypt is deprecating it, which would make server-side stapling hard to use. Review also found open design work: how the client validates the signature on the OCSP response, multi-stapling of the chain, interaction with CRLs, and the callback error codes.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It is indeed, if it ends up deprecated server-side among the big providers then support for it risks being very hard to use.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Disallow infinite endpoints in generate_series() for timestamps."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Disallow infinite endpoints in generate_series() for timestamps."
Reverted commit(s): Disallow infinite endpoints in generate_series() for timestamps.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit eafdf9de06e9b60168f5e47cedcfceecdc6d4b5f
and its back-branch counterparts.  Corey Huinker pointed out that
we'd discussed this exact change back in 2016 and rejected it,
on the grounds that there's at least one usage pattern with LIMIT
where an infinite endpoint can usefully be used.  Perhaps that
argument needs to be re-litigated, but there's no time left before
our back-branch releases.  To keep our options open, restore the
status quo ante; if we do end up deciding to change things, waiting
one more quarter won't hurt anything.

Rather than just doing a straight revert, I added a new test case
demonstrating the usage with LIMIT.  That'll at least remind us of
the issue if we forget again.

precedents_retrieved.title: Built-in connection pooler
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a connection pooler inside Postgres, with proxy worker processes that accept clients on a separate port and multiplex them over a small pool of backends per database and user. A session that changes session state, such as temporary tables, prepared statements or GUCs, is marked tainted and keeps a dedicated backend until the client disconnects.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why the entry was closed in 2021. An earlier commitfest entry was returned in 2020 because the patch needed a rebase and had waited on author for 6 weeks. After the 2021 resubmission, Antonin Houska reported that the patch did not apply to master and raised design issues, including the proxy's use of libpq inside the server, the static connection_proxies setting, walsender connections and unsynchronized shared memory; no reply from the author is shown.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
precedents_retrieved.authors: Michael Paquier, Alexander Korotkov, Simon Riggs
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
Reverted commit(s): Fix handling of orphaned 2PC files in the future at recovery; Fix failures with incorrect epoch handling for 2PC files at recovery; Make use FullTransactionId in 2PC filenames; Speedup 2PC recovery by skipping two phase state files in normal path
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 8f67f994e8ea (down to v13) and c3de0f9eed38 (down to
v17), as these are proving to not be completely correct regarding two
aspects:
- In v17 and newer branches, c3de0f9eed38's check for epoch handling is
incorrect, and does not correctly handle frozen epochs.  A logic closer
to widen_snapshot_xid() should be used.  The 2PC code should try to
integrate deeper with FullTransactionIds, 5a1dfde8334b being not enough.
- In v13 and newer branches, 8f67f994e8ea is a workaround for the real
issue, which is that we should not attempt CLOG lookups without reaching
consistency.  This exists since 728bd991c3c4, and this is reachable with
ProcessTwoPhaseBuffer() called by restoreTwoPhaseData() at the beginning
of recovery.

Per discussion with Noah Misch.

precedents_retrieved.title: Redacting information from logs
precedents_retrieved.summary: Redact every %s argument in ereport() output with a special redaction mode in snprintf.c, and produce both redacted and plain messages. Each log destination would get one version, emit_log_hook would see both, and a custom redaction function, such as a hash, could replace the default.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected that snprintf.c is too low a layer for redaction, because frontend and backend code and non-error paths use it, and because messages built with appendStringInfoString() bypass it. Tomas Vondra argued that most %s arguments are object names or file names, so redacting all of them would make the logs useless. The discussion moved to a structured errparam() design with per-parameter redaction, which still had open problems: type safety, loss of gcc format warnings and translator tools. The visible messages do not show why the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Nor do I think that snprintf.c is a good layer to perform redaction - it's too low level.

precedents_retrieved.title: Show subtransaction overflow status
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch exposes each backend's subtransaction count and whether its subtransaction cache has overflowed, so DBAs can find the sessions that force SLRU lookups for all concurrent queries. It started as two new pg_stat_activity columns and was reworked into a single function returning a record per backend.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that effort should go into fixing the subtransaction overflow performance problem itself, because monitoring does not relieve the problem and could cause compatibility problems once a fundamental fix changes how this area works. Andres Freund agreed and asked for the entry to be marked rejected, also noting it had been failing on cfbot for weeks. The author agreed that a real fix would make the status reporting pointless and marked it rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If the subxact overflow business is causing
real-world performance problems, let's find a way to fix that, not put
effort into monitoring tools that do little to actually alleviate anyone's
pain.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use SIGIO to detect postmaster death
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch uses SIGIO, set up with fcntl(O_ASYNC) and F_SETOWN on the postmaster death pipe, so backends get a signal when the postmaster exits. This gives a postmaster death signal on systems without USE_POSTMASTER_DEATH_SIGNAL, such as macOS and the BSDs.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch after finding that only the last backend to call F_SETOWN on the shared pipe receives the signal. A fix would need a separate pipe per backend, which he judged unwarranted at that point. Heikki Linnakangas and Tom Lane had reviewed it without objection.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
On closer inspection, only the last backend to start up and do
F_SETOWN on the pipe receives the signal.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add LWLock blocker(s) information
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the last holder PID, the last holder mode and the number of holders to each LWLock, and copies this data into the waiting backend's PGPROC. A new function, pg_lwlock_blocking_pid, shows this blocker information for a backend that waits on an LWLock.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas and Andres Freund objected to making LWLock bigger; the patch adds about 12 bytes, which works against past effort to fit BufferDesc into one cache line. Both doubted that the patch has no cost under heavy LWLock contention. Robert Haas also asked how much it adds over sampling wait events, and Andres Freund said such cases need stack information, which an external script can collect. Heikki Linnakangas closed the entry, citing this consensus.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There's been significant work done over the years to get the size of
an LWLock down; I'm not very enthusiastic about making it bigger
again.

precedents_retrieved.title: Built-in connection proxy
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a built-in connection proxy: clients connect to a separate port (6543 by default), and proxy workers spread their sessions over a small pool of backends. A backend whose session changes state (GUCs, temporary tables, prepared statements) is marked tainted and stays dedicated to that client.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with Feedback because the patch needed another rebase and had been Waiting on Author for six weeks. The author had posted a rebased patch on 2020-07-02 but did not change the status, and he did not notice it stopped applying. Earlier reviews raised open design issues: pool limits that are per proxy and not global, too little monitoring, coarse tainting, and a busy loop with poll().
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This needs again a rebase, and has been waiting on author for 6 weeks
now, so I am switching it to RwF.

precedents_retrieved.title: add timing information to pg_upgrade
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the elapsed time of each pg_upgrade step to the status output, for example "ok (took 82 ms)", formatted like psql's PrintTiming(). The goal was to show where upgrade time goes and to measure future work on reducing pg_upgrade downtime.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut questioned who besides developers would use the timings and said pg_upgrade output already has too much information that users cannot act on. He suggested that shell tools such as "pg_upgrade | ts" or "ts -i" are enough, and the author agreed to leave it at that unless someone saw a reason to build it in. Only a related fix that raised MESSAGE_WIDTH to 62 was committed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If it's just for developers and expert users, perhaps existing
shell-level functionality like "pg_upgrade | ts" would suffice?

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P14] and [P21] would report server_version_num to clients that are already connected through the Postgres protocol, which is a different idea from unauthenticated HTTP replies, and neither row records a reason. The thread cites no earlier hackers discussion; message #1 links only to a blog post about guessing the version.
Precedents P14 and P21 cover reporting the server version to authenticated clients and have no recorded reason, so none were cited.
The patch adds no on-disk, WAL or catalog state beyond one GUC. Objections are limited to role semantics across nodes and the wire protocol.
Pre-authentication DoS is not raised. Each request forks and is bounded by a send timeout, much like a normal pre-authentication connection, and the material gives no numbers either way.
Precedents P14 and P21 have no recorded reason and concern GUC_REPORT for the version number, so they do not support these objections.
Precedents P14 and P21 concern sending server_version_num to clients, but no reason is recorded, so they are not used.
The precedents [P14] and [P21] are about reporting server_version_num to clients, but no reason is recorded for either, so neither is cited here.
